title: Nominative Case — Nouns
grammarPoint: Noun gender and nominative singular endings in Polish

explanation.text:
Every Polish noun has a **grammatical gender**: masculine (m), feminine (f), or neuter (n). The gender affects endings throughout the whole grammar system. Learning gender with every new noun is essential.

| Gender | Typical ending | Examples |
|--------|---------------|----------|
| Masculine | consonant | kot, dom, pies, student |
| Feminine | -a | kobieta, mama, herbata, Polska |
| Neuter | -o, -e, -ę | okno, morze, imię |

Exceptions exist (e.g. *mężczyzna* ends in -a but is masculine), so always learn gender with the word.

The **nominative case** is the base form — used for the subject of a sentence.
notes: Learn gender with every new noun — it determines all other forms.
Masculine nouns ending in -a (mężczyzna, kolega) are grammatically masculine.
The nominative is the dictionary form and the subject case.

exercises.explanation: 'Herbata' ends in -a — the typical feminine ending. It is a feminine noun.

exercises.prompt: To jest ___. (This is a window.) [okno = neuter]
exercises.hint: Use the nominative (base) form of the neuter noun

exercises.explanation: You heard: 'To jest pies.' — This is a dog. 'Pies' is masculine nominative — the base form after 'to jest'.

exercises.prompt: Build: This is a book. [książka = feminine]
exercises.explanation: 'To jest książka' = This is a book. After 'to jest', the noun stays in the nominative: książka (feminine, ends -a).
'Dziecko' ends in -o — the classic neuter ending. 'Brat' and 'pies' are masculine (consonant endings). 'Siostra' is feminine (-a ending).
